title: The fall
hook: the Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads violently

segments.voice: Yesterday, to Spain and Sindh: two armies at opposite ends of one empire, and the long histories that began there. Your line was: 711. What did you find about a place's Muslim story? Day nine hundred eleven.

"Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." That is a line from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, from a verse addressed to God as the owner of all power. Some readers hear in it a law of history. The Umayyads had ruled from Damascus through everything we've followed these past days: the coins, the offices, the armies at the strait and the Indus. They looked permanent. Then, far to the east, in Khurasan, men began to raise black banners. Today: the fall.
screen: `THOU GIVEST, THOU WITHDRAWEST.` → `THE UMAYYADS LOOKED PERMANENT.` → `BLACK BANNERS IN KHURASAN.`

segments.voice: The movement grew in secret. Its preachers called people to fight for one chosen from the family of Muhammad, and, the histories say, they kept the name of that person hidden. Those who answered the call included people angry at the Umayyads, and some who hoped for a ruler from the line of Ali. A commander called Abu Muslim led the rising in Khurasan, and the black banners moved west. In Kufa, the hidden name was finally spoken. The new caliph was Abu al-Abbas, a descendant of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle. That is where the name Abbasid comes from. Some who had hoped for a descendant of Ali felt the revolution had been taken from them. Then came the battle by the Zab river, in Iraq. The Umayyad caliph, Marwan, was defeated, fled to Egypt, and was killed there. What followed was not merciful. Al-Tabari reports that members of the Umayyad family were hunted down, and that at one gathering where they had been promised safety, they were killed. The histories set this down plainly, and Muslim writers since have not always agreed on how to judge it. So the day carries two things. A dynasty that had come to power at the end of one civil war lost it in another. The verse speaks of power given and withdrawn; the histories record how this power changed hands. Both sit in this story at once. Dynasties fall.
screen: `A HIDDEN NAME FROM THE PROPHET'S FAMILY.` · `THE NAME IS SPOKEN IN KUFA.` · `THE BATTLE BY THE ZAB.` · then, large: `DYNASTIES FALL.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with how power ends. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something in your life that feels permanent: a job, a role, a reputation, a way things have always been at home. Breathe in. Notice that it had a beginning. Breathe out. Let yourself see, gently, that it will have an end too. Don't argue with the thought, and don't sink into it. Just let it be true for a moment. Then ask: if this ended, what would I want to have done well while I held it? If you pray, you can bring that question to God in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The fall. The violent end of Umayyad rule, when the Abbasids, raising black banners in the name of the Prophet's family, took the caliphate. Today's word.
Your line: dynasties fall. Today, in whatever small power you hold, at work or at home, use it once the way you'd want to be remembered. Day nine hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Muslim historians such as al-Tabari record the fall of the Umayyads in detail, and readers still debate how to judge both dynasties.

original.note: Arabic: the Abbasid state, the dynasty that followed the Umayyads.

trapdoor: what you thought: one family of kings replaced another.
what it means: a secret movement in the name of the Prophet's family overthrew the Umayyads by war, and much blood was shed.
what a scholar hears: the hidden candidate, the disappointment of those who hoped for Ali's line, and al-Tabari's plain report of the killings.
